extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, law, and natural-rights theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the nature, limits, and origins of parental power, filial duties, conjugal society, and the distinction between paternal and political authority in classical natural-rights theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental power is not absolute dominion
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental authority, though sometimes called absolute dominion or regal authority by some, is not truly absolute; it is a temporary and limited power tied to the care of children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts the name 'parental' with 'paternal' to show the absurdity of claiming absolute power for fathers alone, and argues that parental power is only appropriate as a discipline necessary for the child's education and preservation, not as perpetual sovereign authority (sects. 53, 64, 65).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental authority is shared by mother and father
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever rule parents have over children belongs equally to both parents (parental power), not exclusively to the father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural citations and reasoning are used to show that obedience and duties bind children to both father and mother; the text rejects doctrines that would vest exclusive legislative or sovereign power in the father (sect. 53, 64–65).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parents' power arises from a duty to care for offspring
rubrics_metrics.description: The power parents have over children arises from their obligation to preserve, nourish, and educate their offspring during infancy and minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because children are born ignorant and helpless, parents must 'inform the mind, and govern the actions' of their young until reason takes its place; this duty (not a proprietorial right) grounds parental authority (sects. 56, 58).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental government is temporary and ends at maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: The bonds of subjection of children to parents are temporary, like 'swaddling clothes', and cease when age and reason render the child capable of self-government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly emphasizes that parental rule terminates when the child attains the use of reason or the legal age of capacity, and that the father's power 'ceases' when the son becomes free (sects. 55, 59, 69).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom requires law and knowledge of that law
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's freedom to dispose of his actions and property is grounded in his capacity to understand the law that guides those choices; one is not free under a law not yet known to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes freedom from license and argues that law is the direction of a free intelligent agent; children are not under such law until reason is promulgated to them, which explains parental governance until that point (sects. 56–59).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incapacity to reason prolongs tutelage
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person never attains the degree of reason sufficient to know the law (e.g., lunatics, idiots), they remain under the tuition and government of others for the whole time their understanding is incapable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is given as an exception to the general rule that tutelage ends with maturity: natural defects that prevent attainment of reason perpetuate guardianship (sect. 60).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between tuition (temporary) and filial honour (perpetual)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two distinct relations: the temporary privilege/duty of tuition (education and discipline) and the perpetual duty/right of honour, respect, support, and gratitude from children to parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses that failure to distinguish these has caused mistakes; tuition ends with minority, whereas honour and support remain obligations throughout life, but do not confer governing power (sects. 66–69, 71).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental power does not include legislative or capital authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents lack the power to make laws, enact penalties reaching life, limb, or estate, or otherwise exercise sovereign judicial punishments over their children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While parents may command and chastise within discipline, they do not possess magistrate powers (e.g., capital punishment) which belong to the civil authority; parental power is disciplinary and educational only (sects. 64–66, 69).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parents may transfer tuition but not the duty of honour
rubrics_metrics.description: A father may place his child's tuition in other hands (e.g., apprenticeship), discharging some obedience, but this does not cancel the perpetual duty of the child to honour their parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The power of commanding ends with nonage and can be alienated; honour and the obligations of filial piety remain intact regardless (sect. 69).

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence by inheritance is a conditional tie, not natural obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: A father's power to oblige obedience via disposition of his estate is not a natural paternal right but a conditional tie: children who accept an inheritance accept the conditions annexed to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that expectations of inheritance create incentives (reward/punishment) over adults' obedience, but this is analogous to any third party promising an estate and thereby influencing behavior, not an inherent paternal dominion (sects. 72–73).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paternal and political powers are distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental (paternal) power and political (sovereign) power are separate in foundation, ends, and scope; paternal authority does not imply political sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each subject who is a father retains paternal power over his children even if he is a subject of a prince; historical emergence of households' rulers becoming political monarchs is explained as consent and convenience, not as proof of paternal right to political power (sects. 71, 74–76).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political authority originates by consent, not by paternal right
rubrics_metrics.description: The text argues that family government could, by tacit consent and convenience, become political government (fathers as rulers), but this is by consent and executive exercise of natural power, not by natural paternal right to rule politically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses hypothetical and historical reasoning to show how household rule could morph into broader rule, but insists this is not proof that all political power derives from paternal authority (sects. 74–76).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal society is a voluntary compact with specific ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage (conjugal society) is a voluntary compact between man and woman, whose chief end is procreation and whose attendant ends include mutual support and provision for their offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjugal ties are explained as justified by necessity and convenience for rearing children; the compact governs mutual obligations and property in service of procreation and maintenance (sect. 78).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of conjugal bond determined by children's needs and consent
rubrics_metrics.description: The conjugal bond ought to last as long as necessary for the nourishment and support of the young; it could be made determinable by consent, time, or conditions unless positive law requires permanence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes natural reasons (frequency of childbirth and prolonged dependency) why conjugal bonds in humans last longer than among many animals, but allows that, where not bound by law, the contract could be limited or dissolvable (sects. 79–81).

rubrics_metrics.name: Husband’s role in conjugal decisions arises from practical considerations, not absolute sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: Where differing wills arise in marriage, final determination 'naturally' falls to the man as the abler and stronger for matters of common interest, but this does not make him an absolute monarch; the wife retains property and some liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The husband’s practical decision-making role is limited to common concerns and does not extend to the wife's proprietary rights or life; civil magistrate only resolves disputes and does not abridge natural rights necessary for marriage's ends (sects. 82–83).
